hints: Look closely at the boundary around the large central nucleus in Fig. 4.1 and compare it with what a light microscope shows as just a single line.
Think about how DNA is packaged inside the nucleus - some regions stain dark and condensed, others stain light and loose - and what an electron beam can separate.
Focus on small gaps in the boundary and what is attached to its outer surface linking it to the protein-secreting cytoplasm around it.
walkthrough:
See the Envelope as Double**
With a light microscope the nucleus looks like it has a single edge. With electrons you can resolve two separate phospholipid bilayers - an inner and an outer nuclear membrane with a small perinuclear space between them.

Add Pores and Chromatin Detail**
The envelope is interrupted by nuclear pores that allow mRNA and proteins to pass. Inside, DNA is not uniform. Dark condensed heterochromatin and light loose euchromatin can be distinguished.

Link to Protein Secretion**
This is a plasma cell making antibody protein, so look at the outer nuclear membrane. It has ribosomes on its cytoplasmic surface and is continuous with rough endoplasmic reticulum, extra detail invisible with light.

Final answer: Double nuclear envelope / two membranes with perinuclear space; nuclear pores / pore complexes present; heterochromatin and euchromatin visible; outer membrane studded with ribosomes and continuous with RER.

hints: Start by recalling the difference between magnification and the ability to see two separate tiny objects as separate.
Recall the numerical limit for a light microscope set by the wavelength of light, about $200\text{ nm}$ or $0.2\mu\text{m}$, and compare the size of ribosomes and ER membranes to this.
walkthrough:
Resolution Controls Detail**
Seeing more detail is not about making things bigger. It is about resolution - the smallest distance apart at which two objects can still be seen as separate. A light microscope uses light with a relatively long wavelength, so its resolution is poor at about $200\text{ nm}$.

Too Small to Disturb Light**
Ribosomes are about $20\text{ nm}$ and single ER membranes are only a few nm thick. Because they are smaller than $200\text{ nm}$ they cannot separately interfere with light waves, so they blur together and remain invisible. An electron beam has a much shorter wavelength and therefore much higher resolution.

Final answer: Light microscope has low / poor resolution of about $200\text{ nm}$; ribosomes, RER and SER membranes are smaller than the limit of resolution so cannot be resolved as separate structures.

hints: Sort events A to F first into interphase versus mitosis by remembering that DNA copying and normal growth happen before chromosomes become visible.
Within interphase, link DNA polymerase making phosphodiester bonds to S phase, and link centriole replication to the gap after DNA has been copied.
For early mitosis, remember the order: chromosomes first condense and become visible, then line up in the middle.
For late mitosis, remember chromatids separate and move to poles in anaphase, then new envelopes form around them in telophase.
Check which two stages in Table 4.1 have no matching description left, remembering each letter can be used only once and two stages must stay blank.
walkthrough:
Place the Interphase Events**
B describes DNA polymerase catalysing phosphodiester bonds. That is DNA replication, so B = S phase. A describes centrioles replicating. Centrioles replicate in G2 after DNA synthesis, so A = G2 phase. There is no description of normal growth and protein synthesis, so G1 phase = blank.

Place Prophase and Metaphase**
C is condensation of chromosomes, which makes them visible at the start of mitosis, so C = prophase. F is chromosomes lining up at the spindle equator, the definition of metaphase, already given.

Place Anaphase, Telophase and Cytokinesis**
E is centromeres / sister chromatids moving towards poles, pulled by spindle fibres, so E = anaphase. D is nuclear envelope reassembling around each set of daughter chromosomes, so D = telophase. No description refers to splitting of cytoplasm, so cytokinesis = blank.
Final answer: G2 phase = A; S phase = B; G1 phase = blank; cytokinesis = blank; prophase = C; anaphase = E; telophase = D; metaphase = F given.

hints: Think about what clonal expansion produces in large numbers first - the short-lived factory cells that release antibody into blood.
Think about the second cell type produced that stays in circulation for years and what that means for remembering the same antigen.
Link both cell types to speed and amount of antibody on second exposure and the effect on symptoms.
walkthrough:
Many Plasma Cells Mean Much Antibody**
One activated B-lymphocyte divides by mitosis to form a clone of genetically identical plasma cells. All secrete the same specific antibody, so a large quantity is available to form antibody-antigen complexes and promote phagocytosis.

Memory Cells Stay for the Future**
The clone also includes memory B-lymphocytes. They are long-lived and remain in circulation. They provide immunological memory of that specific antigen.

Faster Stronger Second Time**
On second exposure to the same pathogen, memory cells rapidly divide into more plasma cells and more memory cells. Antibody is produced faster and reaches a higher concentration than in the primary response, so the pathogen is destroyed before symptoms develop.

Final answer: Clonal expansion produces large numbers of plasma cells that secrete large quantities of specific antibody to bind antigen; produces large numbers of long-lived memory B-lymphocytes giving immunological memory; on re-infection memory cells divide rapidly to plasma cells giving faster secondary response with higher antibody concentration so no illness.

hints: Recall the normal rule that lymphocytes that would react with the body's own molecules are destroyed during development, and consider what happens if this fails.
Apply this to muscle - think about what specific antibodies binding to receptors at the neuromuscular junction would do to signalling.
walkthrough:
Attacking Self**
Normally the immune system only responds to non-self foreign antigens. In autoimmunity, faulty B-lymphocytes that recognise self antigens are not destroyed, so specific antibodies are made against the body's own cells.

Blocking Muscle Signalling in Myasthenia**
In myasthenia gravis the self antigens are acetylcholine receptors on muscle cell surface membranes at the neuromuscular junction. Antibody binding hinders transmitter action and impairs conduction of the nerve impulse, so muscles weaken.

Final answer: Antibodies / immune response produced against self antigens because faulty B-lymphocytes not destroyed; specific antibody binds to self-antigen / acetylcholine receptors on muscle cell membranes at neuromuscular junction, impairing impulse conduction / action of transmitter.
